We also designed a heuristic that produces reasonably short paths quickly. We are given two triangulations T 0 , T ′ T_{0},T^{\prime} and the goal is to find a short path from T 0 T_{0} to T ′ T^{\prime} . We use a greedy approach that iteratively obtains a triangulation T i + 1 T_{i+1} from a triangulation T i T_{i} as follows. Let F F denote the set of possible unit flips in T i T_{i} . More precisely, the elements of F F are pairs e , e ′ e,e^{\prime} of edges such that a unit flip from T i T_{i} removes e e and inserts e ′ e^{\prime} . We then build a graph G ⁡ ( F ) G(F) with vertex set F F and edges between two unit flips that share a triangle. Notice that the possible parallel flips correspond to independent sets in G ⁡ ( F ) G(F) . We assign a weight to the vertices as follows. The weight of a vertex e , e ′ e,e^{\prime} is the number of edges in T ′ T^{\prime} crossed by e ′ e^{\prime} minus the number of edges in T ′ T^{\prime} crossed by e e . Vertices of zero or negative weight are eliminated. We then proceed to greedily find an independent set I I in G ⁡ ( F ) G(F) . We iteratively add to I I the unmarked vertex of maximum weight, breaking ties by minimum degree. We then mark all the vertices in the closed neighborhood of I I . We repeat until all vertices are marked. This iterative approach is repeated until we reach T ′ T^{\prime} , which will happen in O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) flips because of the following Theorem from [ 10 ] . Theorem 7 . eq T^{\prime} , then there exists a unit flip that replaces an edge e ∈ T e\in T by an edge e ′ e^{\prime} such that e e crosses more edges of T ′ T^{\prime} than e ′ e^{\prime} does. We further improve the heuristic using the squeaky wheel paradigm [ 11 ] . Initially, we assign weight 1 1 to every edge. We modify the definition of the weight of a flip as follows. The weight of a flip e , e ′ e,e^{\prime} is the sum of the weights of the edges in T ′ T^{\prime} crossed by e ′ e^{\prime} minus the sum of the weights of the edges in T ′ T^{\prime} crossed by e e . When we reach triangulation T i + 1 = T ′ T_{i+1}=T^{\prime} from a triangulation T i T_{i} we increment the weight of all edges in T ′ T^{\prime} that are not in T i + 1 T_{i+1} . We repeat the greedy algorithm with the new weights, keeping the best solution found. This procedure is repeated multiple times. We start by adding the Delaunay triangulation as a candidate center. We then build other candidate centers by performing flips starting from the Delaunay triangulation. We add the triangulation we obtained to the set of candidate center and repeat the process for a different value of p p . We calculate the paths from the candidate centers to each solution, building a solution pool. For the next step it will be useful to have a small number of unit-flips in the last flip of the path from the input triangulation to the center. To do that, we either use the greedy heuristic or a MaxSAT formulation. To improve the solution pool, we pick a solution from the pool and look at the triangulations that are one flip away from the center in each path. Journal: 5 Conclusion and Open Problems We were surprised that we managed to solve so many instances exactly and how well an heuristic approximates the exact distance. We believe the following factors help explain the strong practical performance: • The short path length that allows a somewhat small number of variables. • A SAT model where most clauses have size 2 2 . • The ability to eliminate many variables through several arguments. • The fact that the happy edges conjecture is either true or at least holds in most practical cases. The short path lengths are somewhat surprising, given that an Ω ⁡ ( n ) \Omega(n) lower bound is presented in [ 9 ] , in contrast to the Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) \Theta(\log n) bound for combinatorial triangulations [ 12 ] , where we are allowed to flip non-convex quadrilaterals. In the challenge instances, we observed path lengths that are roughly O ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) O(\log n) . Still, there are random instances with only 160 160 points and 20 20 input triangulations and woc instances with only 185 185 points and 6 6 triangulations that we could not solve exactly. Also, we still managed to improve solutions to instances with as few as 320 320 points and 20 20 input triangulations months after the beginning of the challenge. The challenge instances did not have many points in convex position. Surprisingly, the case where all points are in convex position is the hardest for our SAT formulation, as there are Θ ⁡ ( n 4 ) \Theta(n^{4}) empty convex quadrilaterals. We wonder if a different model works better when all and also when most points are in convex position. We believe that the same problem with unit flips is significantly harder because the long path lengths make the SAT formulation much more complex and removing a happy edge can reduce a path length from Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Theta(n^{2}) to Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(n) . Many theoretical open problems remain, such as proving Conjecture 3 . We also wonder if parallel flip distance problem is NP-hard in general and in convex position, as well as the unit flip distance problem in the convex case (the problem is NP-hard for general point sets [ 14 ] ). We also do not know if the problem of calculating b ⁡ ( s ) b(s) (see Section ) can be solved in polynomial time, possibly using dynamic programming.

approximates the exact distance. we believe the following factors help explain the strong practical performance: • the short path length that allows a somewhat small number of variables. • a sat model where most clauses have size 2 2 . • the ability to eliminate many variables through several arguments. • the fact that the happy edges conjecture is either true or at least holds in most practical cases. the short path lengths are somewhat surprising, given that an ω ⁡ ( n ) \omega(n) lower bound is presented in [ 9 ] , in contrast to the θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) 	heta(\log n) bound for combinatorial triangulations [ 12 ] , where we are allowed to flip non-convex quadrilaterals. in the challenge instances, we observed path lengths that are roughly o ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) o(\log n) . still, there are random instances with only 160 160 points and 20 20 input triangulations and woc instances with only 185 185 points and 6 6 triangulations that we could not solve exactly. also, we still managed to improve solutions to instances with as few as 320 320 points and 20 20 input triangulations months after the beginning of the challenge. the challenge instances did not have many points in convex position. surprisingly, the case where all points are in convex position is the hardest for our sat formulation, as there are θ ⁡ ( n 4 ) 	heta(n^{4}) empty convex quadrilaterals. we wonder if a different model works better when all and also when most points are in convex position. we believe that the same problem with unit flips is significantly harder because the long path lengths make the sat formulation much more complex and removing a happy edge can reduce a path length from θ ⁡ ( n 2 ) 	heta(n^{2}) to θ ⁡ ( n ) 	heta(n) . many theoretical open problems remain, such as proving conjecture 3 . we also wonder if parallel flip distance problem is np-hard in general and in convex position, as well as the unit flip distance problem in the convex case (the problem is np-hard for general point sets [ 14 ] ). we also do not know if the problem of calculating b ⁡ ( s ) b(s) (see section ) can be solved in polynomial time, possibly using dynamic programming.

Abstract

Achieving scalable coordination in large robotic swarms is often constrained by reliance on inter-agent communication, which introduces latency, bandwidth limitations, and vulnerability to failure. To address this gap, a decentralized approach for outer-loop control of large multi-agent systems based on the paradigm of how a fluid moves through a volume is proposed and evaluated. A relationship between fundamental fluidic element properties and individual robotic agent states is developed such that the corresponding swarm "flows" through a space, akin to a fluid when forced via a pressure boundary condition. By ascribing fluid-like properties to subsets of agents, the swarm evolves collectively while maintaining desirable structure and coherence without explicit communication of agent states within or outside of the swarm.
